clue.text: Quickly moves goods through part of the UK

indicators.note: the goods are passed through the middle of the region named, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Wales is one of the four nations of the United Kingdom
G is short for good, so two goods give two Gs

explanation.surface: A haulier speeds a consignment through Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: To waggle something is to shake it rapidly to and fro, a brisk back-and-forth motion.

clue.text: Clean hands? Wow, that's unusual

indicators.note: unusual tells us the letters of the two words before it come out in a strange new order

explanation.surface: Someone is amazed to see a pair of hands that are actually clean.
explanation.walkthrough: HANDS and WOW together are rearranged by 'that's unusual'. 'Clean' reads as an adjective but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To wash something down is to give it a thorough rinse with water, the scrub given to a deck or a yard.

clue.text: Centre avoided by gay male? Yes and no

indicators.note: the central letter of the word gay is skipped, leaving only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A joking question about whether gay men steer clear of the fitness centre, answered both ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yes and no' is the setter's wink: 'Centre' is both the definition and the part of GAY that is left out, so the answer is avoided and not avoided at once.
explanation.definitionFit: A gym is a fitness centre, a place to exercise.

clue.text: Shakespearian character in Lear staggering onto set, drunk

indicators.note: a staggering person lurches, so the letters of Lear are thrown about
drunk suggests the letters of set reeling into a new order

explanation.surface: An actor playing King Lear lurches tipsily on to the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staggering' turns LEAR into LAER, and 'drunk' turns SET into TES.
explanation.definitionFit: Laertes is Polonius's son in Hamlet, who fights the prince in the final duel.

clue.text: Sporty type, one involved in hikes uphill, avoiding summit

indicators.note: the numeral one is caught up inside the other piece, so it is placed within it
in a down clue going uphill means the letters are read from bottom to top, backwards
summit is the top letter of the word, which is left out

parts.note: hikes are long walks, treks
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An athletic person goes on hikes up mountains but never reaches the peak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'avoiding summit' drops the T of TREKS, 'uphill' turns REKS into SKER, and 'involved in' puts I inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A skier is someone who takes part in a snow sport, so an athletic person.

clue.text: Bishop — good man in Rome — converted Sicilian criminal perhaps

indicators.note: converted means changed into another form, here the letters of the pieces are rearranged

parts.note: B is the chess notation for bishop
ST, saint, is a good man in crossword convention
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bishop, a holy man of Rome, has been converted to a new faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'converted' shuffles B, ST and ROME together. 'perhaps' marks a Sicilian criminal as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mafia member from Sicily is the classic example of a gangster.

clue.text: Outlaw maid inhales endless pot, a sort of drug

indicators.note: something inhaled is taken inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: Maid Marian is the companion of the outlaw Robin Hood

indicators.note: the last letter of the word is removed

parts.note: a jug is a pot for pouring

explanation.surface: Robin Hood's sweetheart is caught smoking pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlaw maid' is Maid Marian, the heroine of the English legend of Robin Hood, the outlaw of Sherwood Forest; 'endless' and 'inhales' work on the pot inside her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Marijuana is cannabis, a narcotic smoked for its effect.

clue.text: Howl terribly at first, if pierced by one?

definitions.text: Howl terribly at first, if pierced by one?

indicators.note: a thing pierced has something driven into it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: to bay is to howl like a hound

indicators.note: only the opening letter of terribly is wanted

parts.note: taken as written, spelt out

explanation.surface: You would scream horribly if stabbed with one.
explanation.walkthrough: BAY plus T (from 'terribly at first') is 'pierced by' ONE. Read whole, the clue describes the weapon: you would howl if stabbed with it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bayonet is the blade fixed to a rifle's muzzle, used to stab.

clue.text: Be first to steal some piping?

explanation.definitionFit: To head a race is to be in front; read literally, the phrase is to pinch lead, the metal of old water pipes.

clue.text: Parts of Montrose recently promoted as holiday town

indicators.note: in a down clue promoted means moved up, so the letters read upwards, backwards
parts of the two words are taken, a run of letters within them

explanation.surface: Bits of the Scottish town of Montrose have lately been marketed to holidaymakers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts of' takes TROSER from 'monTROSE Recently', and 'promoted' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A resort is a town people visit on holiday, such as a seaside spot.

clue.text: No end of Merlot and semi-petillant wine served by him?

indicators.note: petillant means lightly sparkling, so the letters fizz into a new order
the final letter of Merlot is dropped

explanation.surface: A wine list offers Merlot and a slightly sparkling white.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of' cuts Merlot to MERLO; 'petillant' shuffles MERLO and SEMI together. The definition is a cryptic description of the wine waiter.
explanation.definitionFit: A sommelier is the wine steward in a restaurant who serves bottles to diners.

clue.text: Fine is about a thousand pounds? Crumbs!

indicators.note: the first word goes around the others, so they sit inside it

parts.note: yes, as in 'fine, agreed'
a is one, the Roman numeral I
K, a grand, is slang for a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: Someone is shocked at a thousand-pound penalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is about' puts I and K inside YES.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise or alarm.

clue.text: One involved in discussion about time in retirement? The reverse

indicators.note: the reverse tells us to read the whole string just built backwards

parts.note: RE is Latin for about, concerning
having retired for the night, in bed

explanation.surface: A speaker in a debate wants to raise when people should go to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: RE, T and ABED give RETABED, and 'The reverse' reads it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A debater argues one side in a formal argument.

clue.text: Stuck in mountain in east, order a drink

indicators.note: something stuck in is lodged inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a ben is a Scottish mountain
taken as written
an edict is an official order

explanation.surface: Someone stranded on a peak in the east orders a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: A ben is a Scottish mountain, as in Ben Nevis. 'Stuck in' is the container signal, so the second 'in' is the one that supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Benedictine is a herbal liqueur first made by monks in Normandy.

clue.text: Caretaker rushed about endlessly after bank holiday

indicators.note: the second piece follows the first in the answer

parts.note: Jan 1, New Year's Day, is a bank holiday

indicators.note: the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to tear about is to rush around

explanation.surface: A caretaker dashes around after the holiday break.
explanation.walkthrough: January 1, New Year's Day, is a public holiday in Britain, written as month plus Roman numeral; 'endlessly' trims the rushing verb and 'after' puts it behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A janitor looks after a building, as a caretaker does.

clue.text: Barbara repeatedly found in royal residence

parts.note: two famous Barbaras: the actress Barbara Windsor and the Labour politician Barbara Castle
two famous Barbaras: the actress Barbara Windsor and the Labour politician Barbara Castle

explanation.surface: An actress called Barbara keeps turning up at a palace.
explanation.walkthrough: Barbara Windsor was a British comic actress (Carry On films, EastEnders); Barbara Castle was a Labour cabinet minister. 'repeatedly' says use two Barbaras.
explanation.definitionFit: The castle in Berkshire is an official home of the British monarch.

clue.text: Old-fashioned, small skating area used by Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner, the Oxford don famed for swapping word beginnings, signals the first letters are exchanged

parts.note: dinky means small and neat
a rink is an ice skating area

explanation.surface: The old professor describes a quaint little ice rink.
explanation.walkthrough: DINKY RINK with first sounds swapped. Dinky is British for small and cute.
explanation.definitionFit: Rinky-dink is slang for outmoded, shabby or second-rate.

clue.text: Protesters finally tried surrounding new airport

indicators.note: only the last letter of protesters is wanted
the word for tried goes around the other piece

parts.note: to try food is to taste it

explanation.surface: Campaigners at last tried to encircle a new airport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' gives S; 'surrounding' puts N inside TASTED. Stansted is a London airport in Essex, long opposed by protesters.
explanation.definitionFit: Stansted is one of the airports serving London.

clue.text: Separation? Quite the opposite, as announced in Feb 1981

definitions.text: Quite the opposite, as announced in Feb 1981

explanation.definitionFit: Disengagement means a parting or withdrawal; read as Di's engagement, it is the betrothal of Lady Diana Spencer to Prince Charles, made public in February 1981.

clue.text: Portuguese town welcomes a legendary singer

indicators.note: a town welcoming someone takes them in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Sintra is a hill town near Lisbon

explanation.surface: A town in Portugal greets a famous crooner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'welcomes' puts A inside SINTRA.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Sinatra was an iconic American crooner.

clue.text: Demanding fellow should be added to English team

indicators.note: the fellow is attached after the other pieces, so the charade runs in that order

parts.note: XI, eleven, is a cricket or football team
a gent is a man, a fellow

explanation.surface: A selector insists a certain chap join the England side.
explanation.walkthrough: XI is a team of eleven players.
explanation.definitionFit: Exigent describes something pressing, needing urgent attention.

clue.text: Likely source of danger which lurks round about

indicators.note: the first word is placed around the next, which sits inside it

parts.note: that, as a relative pronoun, can stand for which
RE means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Something menacing hides nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'which' looks like a link to the definition but supplies letters; 'lurks round' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A menace is a possible cause of harm.

clue.text: Journalist's wish to go round in horse-drawn carriage

parts.note: a hack is a journalist

indicators.note: going round means turning back, so the letters of the word for wish are read backwards

parts.note: a yen is a longing or wish

explanation.surface: A reporter wants a ride in a horse and trap.
explanation.walkthrough: A hackney carriage is also the official British name for a taxi; 'to go round' turns the longing word backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A hackney is a horse-drawn cab for hire.

clue.text: Briefly assumed editor blundered with noun

indicators.note: a blunder is a mistake, so the letters of editor go wrong into a new order

parts.note: N is the grammar abbreviation for noun

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor made a grammar slip with a noun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blundered' rearranges EDITOR into TRIEDO.
explanation.definitionFit: To put on a garment for a moment, to check the fit, is to try it on.

clue.text: Belgian location's no place for an idiot

indicators.note: there is no room left for the word an, so it is removed

parts.note: Antwerp is a port city in Belgium

explanation.surface: A Belgian city is unsuitable for a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no place for' takes AN out of ANTWERP: the clue's 'an' is the letters removed, not an article.
explanation.definitionFit: A twerp is a silly or annoying person, a fool.

clue.text: Be spotted beginning to get stuck in doorway

indicators.note: one piece lodges inside the other

parts.note: an exit is a doorway out

indicators.note: only the first letter of spotted is wanted

explanation.surface: Someone is seen when getting jammed in a door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spotted beginning' gives S, and 'to get stuck in' puts it inside EXIT. 'Be spotted' reads as one phrase, but 'Be' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To exist is to have being, to live.

clue.text: A book collection begins with popular poem that's short and unrefined

indicators.note: the first pieces come before the rest in the answer

parts.note: in means fashionable, popular

indicators.note: short means the word is cut by its last letter

parts.note: an elegy is a mournful poem
NT, the New Testament, is a collection of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A book anthology opens with a well-liked brief poem but lacks polish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's short' trims the mournful poem by one letter, and 'begins with' puts the popular word and that poem ahead of A and the Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: Inelegant means lacking grace or polish, coarse.

clue.text: For instance, hard type of wood

parts.note: as, as in 'such as', introduces an example
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Hard timber, for example.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash is a tree whose pale, tough timber is used for tool handles.

clue.text: Decorated strip player sported at match

indicators.note: the player appears at the match, standing right next to it in the answer

parts.note: a tie is a cup match
a back is a defensive player in football or rugby

explanation.surface: A footballer wears a fancy kit at a cup game.
explanation.walkthrough: A TIE is a knockout cup match in British football.
explanation.definitionFit: A tieback is an ornamental band of fabric holding a curtain to one side.

clue.text: Mislaid the cap daughter mended

indicators.note: mislaid means put in the wrong place, so the letters of the cap are placed in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone lost a hat that their daughter had repaired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mislaid' rearranges THE CAP into PATCHE.
explanation.definitionFit: Patched means repaired with a piece of material.
